title: Genetic Medicines For Kidney Diseases: Jason Coloma on The Long Run - TimmermanReport.com
gist: Podcast show notes for a Long Run episode with Maze Therapeutics CEO Jason Coloma, whose South San Francisco company runs human-genetics-driven small molecule discovery for kidney disease. The investable content is thin but specific: Maze has two lead programs, an APOL1-directed kidney drug and an SLC6a19 program, both facing Phase II readouts within roughly the next year, after the company IPO'd in early 2025 and rebuilt a partnership that the federal government moved to block on antitrust grounds.

insights.claim: Maze Therapeutics has two lead programs - an APOL1-directed kidney drug and a second aimed at SLC6a19 - and expects to learn within roughly the next year whether they clear Phase II clinical trial scrutiny.
insights.speaker: @ldtimmerman
insights.so_what: Two binary Phase II readouts inside twelve months on a single small-cap makes this a dated-catalyst name rather than a story stock; position sizing should assume gap risk in both directions.
insights.quote: Maze is now in position to find out in the next year or so whether its two lead programs – an APOL1 directed kidney drug and another aimed at SLC6a19 – are good enough to pass Phase II clinical trial scrutiny.
insights.locator: Those battles have strengthened the company culture

insights.claim: Maze is pursuing kidney disease with small molecule drugs intended to halt or potentially reverse disease progression, rather than the cell or gene therapy modalities usually attached to genetic-medicine framing.
insights.speaker: @ldtimmerman
insights.so_what: Small molecules carry conventional manufacturing and reimbursement economics, so a genetics-derived small molecule sidesteps the COGS and delivery risks that weigh on gene-therapy valuations for the same target biology.
insights.quote: The company is developing small molecule drugs to halt or potentially reverse kidney diseases.
insights.locator: Jason is the CEO of South San Francisco-based Maze Therapeutics

insights.claim: Maze's discovery approach mines large pools of human genetic data for variants that either cause disease or protect against it, using protective variants as the starting point for drug targets rather than beginning from disease pathways.
insights.speaker: @ldtimmerman
insights.so_what: Human-genetics-anchored targets historically carry higher clinical success rates than pathway-derived ones; it is the main reason to underwrite the pipeline ahead of data.
insights.quote: looking at large pools of data to see how variants of one kind or another can make people sick, or protect them from falling ill
insights.locator: The drug discovery work at Maze is grounded in human genetics

themes.theme: Antitrust as a biotech deal risk

insights.claim: An important Maze partnership unraveled after the federal government sought to block it on antitrust grounds, and the company subsequently secured a different partner to support the same program.
insights.speaker: @ldtimmerman
insights.so_what: Antitrust intervention reaching down to individual biotech licensing deals is a live risk factor for partnership-dependent small caps; it lengthens deal timelines and weakens negotiating leverage with large-pharma partners.
insights.quote: An important partnership unraveled after the federal government sought to block it on antitrust grounds.

insights.claim: Maze went public in early 2025 only after surviving several lean years of biotech financing, positioning it as a company that cleared the funding drought rather than one that IPO'd into an easy window.
insights.speaker: @ldtimmerman
insights.so_what: Companies that survived the 2022-2024 biotech funding winter tend to carry leaner cost structures and disciplined capital plans - relevant when comparing cash runway against the coming Phase II readouts.
insights.quote: Maze went public in early 2025, after surviving several lean years of biotech financing.
